subject: Computer Networking
title: Email: An Accidental Killer App
description: A short lesson to help you apply Email: An Accidental Killer App.

hook.text: ARPANET was built for sharing computing resources. Instead, people used it to send each other messages.

buildup.text: In 1971, Ray Tomlinson wrote a program to send text between machines. He chose '@' to separate user from host.

discovery.text: Email exploded in popularity. Within two years, it accounted for 75% of all ARPANET traffic.

twist.text: Nobody planned for email to dominate. The network was designed for remote computing, not personal messages.

climax.text: Email proved that networks are most valuable for communication — a lesson that shaped every future network.

punchline.text: Email wasn't the plan. It became the point.

quiz.question: Who introduced the '@' symbol for email addresses?

details.summary: Email was created by Ray Tomlinson in 1971 as a quick hack to send messages between ARPANET users. It was never planned as a major application, but it quickly became the network's most popular use. Email drove adoption of networking and remains the most widely used internet application.
details.whyItMatters: Email became the first killer app of networking, driving adoption far more than the resource-sharing that ARPANET was designed for. It proved that communication is the killer use case for networks.
takeaways: Ray Tomlinson created email and the @ symbol convention in 1971
Email was not a planned ARPANET application
It quickly became the most popular use of the network

faq.question: Why did email become more popular than resource sharing?
faq.answer: ARPANET was built to share expensive computing resources. But human communication turned out to be far more compelling than accessing remote computers. Email was instant, asynchronous, and required no coordination. It was the text messaging of its era.

faq.question: Why did Tomlinson choose the @ symbol?
faq.answer: He needed a symbol that would not appear in anyone's name to separate the user from the host. The @ symbol was rarely used in computing and naturally read as user at host. It was a pragmatic choice that became one of the most recognized symbols worldwide.
